books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: James K. Polk, Inaugural Address, March 4, 1845

stimulus.source_note: James K. Polk, Inaugural Address, March 4, 1845. Public domain.
stimulus.text: Texas was once a part of our country — was unwisely ceded away to a foreign power — is now independent, and possesses an undoubted right to dispose of a part or the whole of her territory and to merge her sovereignty as a separate and independent state in ours... To enlarge its limits is to extend the dominions of peace over additional territories and increasing millions... Nor will it become in a less degree my duty to assert and maintain by all constitutional means the right of the United States to that portion of our territory which lies beyond the Rocky Mountains. Our title to the country of the Oregon is “clear and unquestionable,” and already are our people preparing to perfect that title by occupying it with their wives and children.

source: original; stimulus is a verbatim excerpt from James K. Polk, Inaugural Address, March 4, 1845, public domain
stem: Polk's claim about Oregon in the passage most directly reflects which of the following?

options.text: A treaty already signed with Britain dividing Oregon at the 49th parallel.
options.misconception: No treaty had been signed when Polk spoke; the Oregon Treaty came in June 1846.

options.text: The belief that American settlement strengthened the United States' claim to the land.
A Supreme Court decision awarding Oregon to the United States.
options.misconception: No court decided the Oregon question; it was settled by diplomacy.

options.text: An agreement with Russia to buy its claims in the Pacific Northwest.
options.misconception: Russia had already withdrawn its claims south of 54°40′ in 1824; nothing was bought from Russia.

rationales.A: Polk spoke in March 1845, and the Oregon Treaty dividing the territory at the 49th parallel was not signed until June 1846. Background: Britain's earlier counter-proposal had been the Columbia River.
rationales.B: Polk says Americans are “preparing to perfect that title by occupying it with their wives and children” — settlement, in his words, makes the claim real.
rationales.C: The Oregon boundary was a diplomatic dispute with Britain, never decided by the Supreme Court.
rationales.D: Russia gave up its claims below 54°40′ by treaty in 1824; the United States bought nothing from Russia in the Northwest.
rationales.general:
1. Read what Polk says about Oregon. The title is “clear and unquestionable,” and Americans are preparing to “perfect that title by occupying it.”
2. Ask what perfects a title. For Polk, it is families moving in and living on the land.
3. Rule out the rest. No treaty, court, or purchase existed in March 1845.
Remember: in the 1840s, planting settlers on disputed land was treated as a kind of proof — feet on the ground backed the claim on paper.
